classification.difficultyReason: Combine the positivity restriction on a logarithmic argument with a rational substitution, recognise squared binomial factors, and justify the logarithm power law on the original domain to prove the identity.

inlines.text: A function name does not have to be a single letter. In this case the function has been given the name ‘ath’ because it is related to the arc hyperbolic tangent, which is studied in some university courses.

answer.worked:
The logarithm requires $\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}>0$. The numerator and denominator must have the same sign.

Both are positive when $x>-1$ and $x<1$. Both cannot be negative, since that would require $x<-1$ and $x>1$.

Hence the domain is $(-1,1)$.

answer.short:
$\operatorname{ath}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)=2\operatorname{ath}(x)$ for $-1<x<1$.

Substitution gives the logarithm of $\left(\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}\right)^2$; apply the power law.
answer.worked:
For $-1<x<1$, put $u=\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}$. Since
$$u+1=\frac{(x+1)^2}{1+x^2}>0,\qquad 1-u=\frac{(x-1)^2}{1+x^2}>0,$$
we have $-1<u<1$, so the substitution is defined. Also $\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}>0$.
$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{ath}\left(\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)&=\log_2\left(\frac{1+\frac{2x}{1+x^2}}{1-\frac{2x}{1+x^2}}\right)\\\operatorname{ath}\left(\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)&=\log_2\left(\frac{1+x^2+2x}{1+x^2-2x}\right)\\\operatorname{ath}\left(\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)&=\log_2\left(\frac{(1+x)^2}{(1-x)^2}\right)\\\operatorname{ath}\left(\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)&=2\log_2\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)\\\operatorname{ath}\left(\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)&=2\operatorname{ath}(x).\end{align*}$$
